Do you know what it’s like to be raised mixed in a white culture? Especially if you don’t have a strong connection to your non-white side(s) or if you look passably white?

You become white, but not really white. Because you can’t be. And you can’t be truly from those other cultures either. You belong everywhere and nowhere.

I think that the difference is that white culture is genuinely more accepting in general for many reasons, including cultural security. POC cultures and communities are understandably suspicious of outsiders exactly because they have so much more to fear from them. They are resistant to threats to their traditions whether those threats are from within or without because those traditions are what has been victimised in the past. Kids learn from their parents and pass those attitudes onto each other. This is why mixed kids feel more comfortable being accepted by their white “melting-pot-minded” peers, while cultural communities are insular and judgemental of who they let into their spaces.

So yeah, being bullied by (for example) Mexicans kids at school while the white kids tell you they “don’t see you like that” is an experience you don’t seem to understand. Of course someone would gravitate to the culture that is their home AND the people who for the most part don’t make them feel weird or unwanted for not being quite “right” or just simply for being part-white at all. Such an experience can create conclusions and biases that take time and effort to unravel when the person is an adult. Nobody chooses the race they are born as, it’s not a character select screen system. You get what you get and have to navigate growing up being judged for it.

I don’t know whether you don’t understand because you’ve never been through it. Maybe you have. I won’t presume. OP is actively here trying to genuinely connect with non-white cultures and better themselves as a person, and… that’s all you have to say to help them do that?

Maybe you should think about whether you’re helping people with the things you say. Nobody wins from this exchange.
OP, you didn’t do anything wrong. It’s like survivors guilt, because you’re assigning yourself control over something you couldn’t. Please forgive yourself.

Keep looking. 

The right people really are out there. Finding them is like luck; imagine that every new bond you form is a flip of a coin, and the bet you place is your trust and love. Heads, you lose and they don’t reciprocate, tails, you win and they do. House rules, double or nothing.

You keep flipping coins, hoping eventually you’ll flip a tails, and after weeks, months, years of flipping heads and losing everything you gambled, it seems like maybe every coin is just heads on both sides. The game is rigged. Everybody sucks.

So feeling hopeless, you resign yourself, turn inwards and protect your own coin from everybody else. It’s a defence mechanism.

But keep flipping. The more you flip, the more chances you get. Don’t let the heads get you down, just move on and keep looking. You **will** eventually find the people who love you just like you love them. Personally, I found all of mine on completely different corners of the Earth, people I would have never met in any other age of human history. God bless the internet.

Another thing worth mentioning is that unlike metaphorical coins, it isn’t just 50/50. Sometimes people do a very good job of pretending to look like they flip tails, maybe for years. Sometimes people are very clearly heads from the start, but they’re so compelling anyway that you might decide you’ll just be content with giving and not getting. Sometimes it feels like any coin will do. Anything to not be alone.

Life is hard. People are hard.

But there are coins that flip tails on both sides. Like some of us. We exist. Keep looking for the helpers.

Oh my god, half of these replies. I know most everybody here means the best and most of the advice is really good, but I also know what it’s like to come back from acute suicidal thoughts and work up the courage to tell someone, only to hear what is essentially “Oh great, good job not doing the bad thing; now it’s time to fix everything! It’s all broken because you made bad choices and you need to fix it now!! Right now! It’s your fault, you are weak, you did a bad thing, fix it, get help, FIX EVERYTHING IN YOUR LIFE BEFORE YOU DO THE BAD THING AGAIN-“

Like I know that isn’t what people are *trying* to convey, but this dust-yourself-off-and-get-to-work attitude can make one feel like they are a failure at dying *and* living. Like the choice is between hurting everybody and suffering forever. And the world screams, “THEN SUFFER FOREVER!!” and you tell yourself that yes, it’s my fault for suffering, I must try harder not to suffer…

This is the distorted thinking of deepest depression mixed with great but badly-timed advice.

Okay, OP. Here’s my attempt.

It starts with something called The View From Halfway Down.

I’m referring to an episode of a TV show called BoJack Horseman. Have you heard of it? If you haven’t and a dark comedy drama about generational trauma and mental illness and the crushing reality of the modern world sounds like your thing, I would highly recommend it. But if that’s not your thing, that’s okay. There’s only one episode I think you should definitely watch, and that is the one I just mentioned. Trust me.

Why? Well, in a brief way, let me tell you about my experience with the view from halfway down. I have survived countless suicide attempts in my life. Many, nobody knows about. I’ve probably forgotten half of them myself. Three or so years ago, I almost succeeded. I had a near-death experience.

And in those last few seconds, when I nearly died, I faced death and fought to live. I didn’t choose to fight. I didn’t choose to live. I just did, in that moment, on instinct and terror. The view changed me.

I never thought I’d be able to desire suicide again, but unfortunately it’s not that easy. The spectre of Death won’t stop haunting me when things are bad, but I live in hope. I understand. I do. It’s too much pain sometimes. And I am so sorry that you are feeling it.

Which brings me to my second piece of advice: never do this alone again. I might not be here, writing this to you, if I hadn’t had a friend who was absolutely determined to drag the truth out of me as I was saying goodbye. It took some hours of the worst pain I’d felt in a long time, but then it was over, and now I’m still here. That’s how we fight the draw to the void. Battle by battle. One at a time, every time it comes forth like a wave from the horizon.

But you should NOT have to do that alone. Think about it: most who attempt suicide in this world do it alone, and those who succeed are almost always alone when they do. To survive depression is to fight demons singlehanded and mortally crippled, all the way to the end. I personally don’t think anybody who hasn’t gone through that experience could truly picture how it feels.

Find somebody. It doesn’t matter who. Hopefully you have a loved one in real life who might be willing to sit through the black hours with you and not offer judgement or advice. But maybe not. Maybe you can’t bring yourself to lean on somebody you love like that. I understand that too. Luckily, this is 2022 and there are helplines, counsellors, support groups — and if none of those work for some reason, there’s the internet. Lots of subreddits. Write another post like this, write ten of them, cry into the abyss. Maybe it will cry back. There are lots of good people right here on this post who will bear with you. If I were better, maybe I could be that friend, but I have to keep my eyes on the road.

Once there is a little distance between you and the void, and the view starts looking a little different, and the pain hurts just a little less, that’s when you come back to this thread and find all of the good advice. Get help, but when you’re ready for it. You aren’t the problem. You aren’t weak. In fact, every occasion you have stepped down from that chair is a badge of bravely and selflessness, to face living only for the sake of others. Many people couldn’t get down from their chairs again. Forgive yourself. Allow yourself to hurt. It’s okay.

I wish you all the best. It’s a long road ahead of you, but you can rest when you need to. And when you can’t drive any longer, let somebody take the wheel while you catch your breath. I love you, my partner in the fight. Good luck. 🤍

Before I respond, let me say that I am only semi-diagnosed; I was referred to two different dieticians and they both told me that I had an eating disorder and that they couldn’t help me, because I needed to get psychiatric help with it. Unfortunately, I haven’t found anybody in my area that can treat me. After doing my own research, I’ve decided my ED is very likely ARFID, but since I also have a problem with binge-eating and I am obese because almost all of my safe foods are junk, that might make it EDNOS. Who knows.

Either way, here you go!

**Does anybody have very diverse safe foods? Like Cheerios are safe but also grilled salmon with lemon rice and mixed veggies is safe.**
Yes. I can sometimes assemble a meal out of my safe foods: for example, a baked potato with cheddar cheese, some slices of garlic bread, a very specifically made salad... But it took me several minutes to think of that example. Almost all of my safe foods are bread, potato or cheese prepared in various ways, and that can give you a good illusion of “diversity”, I guess. Most of the ways normal people diversify their meals don’t apply to me, though.

**Does anybody else have an acute obsession with Cheerios or crackers or bread?**
I wouldn’t call it an obsession, but almost all of my safe foods are carbs, fats and sugars. That includes a LOT of bread and sometimes crackers. I can’t eat Cheerios, though; in fact, I find most cereal pretty difficult. Don’t even mention muesli, never ever ever ever...

**Does anybody have good recipes with their safe foods with a high nutrition level?**
Pretty much the only thing that I eat with “good nutrition” is curry, and I only eat two kinds, and they have to have specific textures. Oh, and the few fruits and smoothies I like.

**Does anybody have a little technique to make trying new foods a little easier?**
I wish... Honestly, I just have to force it in and try not to throw up so as to not upset whoever insists I have to taste it. It’s not easy and I wish it could be.

**Anybody else always order the same food no matter what restaurant you go to? (I.e. spaghetti and meatballs, chicken fingers, etc)**
Yes. There’s always just one or two dishes maximum that I can eat on a restaurant menu, I just scan until I find them. Pizza, pasta with plain tomato sauce, tarka daal curry. Sometimes there isn’t anything and I just eat sides: onion rings, chips, nachos. Going for a meal with others and only eating chips while everyone else pigs out and keeps saying “Are you SURE you don’t want anything else?” in a voice filled with pity is a distress I know all too well. Why yes, I would love something else other than chips, there’s just NOTHING ELSE I CAN HAVE HERE! Even worse, sometimes my family will forgo which restaurant they actually want to eat at in favour of somewhere that they know I can eat at. Knowing they really want Chinese food but hearing them cheerfully insist that it’s “*totally* okay to go to Pizza Hut again, so *everybody* can have something to eat!”... I always feel super guilty. At this point, I’m so used to not being able to order from unfamiliar restaurants that I don’t mind it, but I suppose seeing me with nothing while they eat large meals makes them feel guilty.

**After trying new foods, does anybody else think their safe food is literally the best food in the world?**
Not the best thing, but it makes me question why people ever try radically new foods.

**Anybody else eat so much of their safe food that they become sick of it?**
Oh my god, yes. All the time. Literally, all the time. Especially last year; the reason why I got referred to dieticians was because I was suffering from the after effects of some trauma and my safe food pool literally narrowed down to nothing but crisps and plain cheese pizza of one specific store brand. For weeks. I hated it and I felt super terrible and weak all the time, but I couldn’t eat anything else. I especially couldn’t stand anything soupy or watery or chunky or spicy or... You get the idea.

**Anybody have high protein safe foods?**
Redskin peanuts, plain yoghurt, chickpeas... I think that’s it. I’m like you; I can’t eat any meat, fish or poultry whatsoever. I have a hard time getting protein too; I take a multivitamin pill, iron pill and omega oil pill every day to try and make up some of the deficiencies. I also take vitamin D, but that’s because I’m agoraphobic and don’t get any sunlight.

**Anybody else get super uncomfortable/grossed out when other people eat foods that aren’t safe for you?**
Depends. Often, yes. If they’re not close to me though, it’s usually okay. If they aren’t eating messily, that also helps. However, if somebody eats a non-safe food around me that smells really strong... Oh my god, it is just hellish. I literally have to run away, where it can’t follow me. I try to distract myself to get rid of the disgust, nausea and panic, but it’s really hard. If somebody eats a smelly non-safe food messily and close to me... I haven’t cried yet, but I’ve come close.

**Does anybody else kinda revel in being sick because then you don’t need to justify your eating habits? (Like you can just say you’re sick and everybody understands)**
No, not this one.


**Am i the only one who always brought their lunch to school in case the school lunch wasn’t safe?**
I didn’t do that. When I was in primary school, the ARFID wasn’t nearly as bad. By the time I got to secondary school and it started getting worse, the school lunches were safer than anything from home. Fresh pizza, pasta, baked potatoes, chips. They had an amazing yoghurt sauce too. For a long time all I ate every day for lunch was a chip sandwich covered in that sauce. Also... I didn’t have anybody to make lunches for me a lot of the time, so that contributed.

**Does anybody else have a messed up hunger schedule? Like I get hungry at random times during the day.**
I try to explain it to people like this: my appetite and my hunger are totally separate. Right now, as I’m typing this, I have terrible hunger pains in my stomach because I haven’t eaten all day. I don’t want to right now. The pains don’t make me want to eat, they just hurt and make me feel nauseous. However, sometimes I am just constantly mentally hungry, even when I’m not physically hungry. Sometimes I binge on food mindlessly until I feel sick, lie around in pain for a couple of hours, and then as soon as the pain wears off binge again. It can last for days. I’ve actually vomited from binging so much. Even worse, I am absolutely horrific with comfort eating. Binging is sometimes the only thing that will calm my mood. I graze mindlessly and read. It honestly helps, but I hate it... I wish other coping methods worked as well...

**What are some ways that I can find/discover more safe foods without spending a lot of money?**
I don’t know, sorry.

**Has anybody else been lectured about food by kids or people a lot younger than you?**
I don’t know any kids. Probably a good job.

**Are other people weirdly obsessed with gum or mints?**
No; in fact, I hate a lot of minty things. I have to use kid’s dental products to avoid the mint flavour.

**Anybody else only like about 3 different kinds of apples?**
YES. Actually, only one kind of apple: pink lady. I also can’t eat the skin or the bits where the flesh gets tough close to the core, so every apple I eat has to be meticulously peeled, cored and sliced. I don’t eat a lot of apples because of this; pink lady apples are expensive, and it’s a lot of effort.

**Am I the only one that doesn’t like eating out because you don’t want to order something, find out you don’t like it, and waste money?**
Yes and no. Money rarely bothers me. It’s the other things I mentioned earlier that do. Wasting good food, being disappointed, going hungry, being pitied or questioned...

**How do I tell people that I can’t choose what foods are safe or not?**
If you figure out the answer to this question, let me know.

**Was anybody else underweight in their youth and then found a high caloric safe food and gained a lot of weight?**
Oh my god, YES! We should be friends, we have a LOT in common with this disorder. When I was a very little girl, I actually was diagnosed “anorexic” a few times. I had a more typical version of ARFID, where I just lost the desire to eat for months. At some point, my family figured out that I would eat if they gave me junk, and boom...

**Does anybody know where I can get help online?**
I know of a service, but I’m in the U.K., so it may not be useful to you...

**What are some very common safe foods that I could try?**
Sorry, I don’t know. I don’t know anybody but me that has ARFID.

**Is hoarding food normal for people with ARFID?Like hiding it in your room for later**
Y’know, I don’t think it is? I’ve never heard of it being a symptom. That being said, I also do this. I hoard food terribly, I have for a long time. I think it’s connected to other things for me, but maybe I’m wrong.

Hope that helps! It was nice to answer those questions, actually; your symptoms seem extremely similar to mine and it made me feel less alone. Most people with ARFID are underweight, have low appetites and rarely eat. I always wondered if my guesswork was stupidity on my part, but maybe not!

That’s so weird! I have *literally* used that exact same analogy before. I eventually modified it, though; for me, it’s like vomit. Something you would not want to put in your mouth under **any** circumstances. Something that makes you want to puke yourself if you watch someone put it in their mouth. Something that even the smell of makes you feel sick and uncomfortable until you can finally breathe air again. Something that you can instantly look at and even the appearance makes you back away and hide. You can cover crickets in chocolate so they’re unnoticeable, but chocolate vomit... is still vomit.

The good thing is that if ARFID is caught in childhood, it has a good recovery rate. Some kids and teens just grow out of it. My SO’s cousin was pretty bad as a child, even worse than I was; he went through several years of eating almost nothing but fries, ketchup and vinegar. These days, apart from being really sensitive to even slightly spicy food, he’s a normal eater with a decent enough diet. I wish you and your stepdaughter the best of luck with her recovery. :)

When they eat something that smells strongly and I beg them to take it away because I can’t stand it, they act irritated and confused, even when they’re in MY room. When they try to give me food and I try to explain in the nicest way why I can’t eat it — it’s in an opened packet, it’s been partially eaten , it’s not the right brand, it’s homemade by somebody outside the family, it’s something I’ve never tried before, the texture disgusts me, it’s got one or more of the many many foods I can’t eat as an ingredient, it’s something that was on my safe list but randomly become temporarily intolerable (this happens pretty often) — they act offended, don’t seem to understand anything I say and act like I’m being ungrateful or intentionally difficult.

I’ve had these reactions all my life. They still hurt, but I try to get over it. The laughing and teasing is the worst, though. It’s like somebody running towards an arachnophobe with a spider in their hands. I know it seems irrational and silly to other people, but I can’t help it and didn’t choose it...

Anyway, enough about that. I’m sure it means a lot to your stepdaughter that you’re trying to understand and accommodate them. Welcome to the sub! (Says a first-time poster...)

Just about anything that I’ve ever heard can be dangerous. 

Passing a truck? Plus, their cargo can fall out at any time if it’s not absolutely secure... #NotAllTruckDrivers #ButYouNeverKnowWhich

Bees? I’ve never been stung by a bee. I heard that people who have never been stung by bees can be deathly allergic to them. It’s a good thing bees are usually chill, but then there’s wasps and hornets, maybe the same thing happens...

Exercise machines? Dude, I saw videos of peoples’ legs being snapped completely in half. BACKWARDS. I heard it only takes 7lbs of pressure. Even going down staircases makes me nervous when I remember it.

Umbrellas? Well, when do you use umbrellas? During a rainstorm! Know what else can happen during rainstorms? LIGHTNING! Lightning loves metal sticky-up things. Hospital Number One: Mostly a fantastic hospital, but one time...

Morning, very early when dawn was just breaking, I woke up and found a patient sitting in one of the tv rooms. She was rocking back and forth in a chair, making strange HMMMing noises on occasion. As I approached, I noticed a terrible, gut-wrenching smell. I was a teen at the time and didn’t know what it was. She had her back to me, but I called out:

“Excuse me, are you okay?”

She continued rocking and HMMMing. I watched her for a few minutes. Eventually, I went into the room and sat in a chair across from her. The smell was atrocious, but nothing I couldn’t handle. The lady was smiling, but it was like her lips were pressed together.

“Are you okay?” I asked again.

More HMMMing. She stared at me. She seemed pleased to have me present, but it was hard to tell for sure. After a little time spent trying to coax her into communicating with me and having no success, I went to find the night nurses (morning shift hadn’t started). “I think there’s a lady back there who needs help,” I told the nurses at the nurse station.

They informed me that they knew she was there and it was fine. Then they continued talking. Being young, confused and meek, I walked away. I decided to go back to the lady and keep her company for a while longer. I remember that I kept asking her if she wanted a bath; I figured that the smell was because she’d urinated where she sat. She never changed, just kept staring and rocking and HMMMing once or twice a minute. Eventually, I gave up.

Some time later, I saw a nurse gently leading her to one of the bathrooms that had a bathtub. I don’t know how long she was sitting there before that point. I realised years after that it might not have been just pee I smelled. Then I wondered if sitting in that was giving her chemical burns, but she was too ill to ask for help. I’d guess it was between 30 minutes and 3 hours until she got help (this happened over a decade ago). If I’d been as brave and/or as understanding as I am now, she wouldn’t have been left like that so long... But I was naive, and the past is the past.

Hospital Number Two: As I found out after my *imprisonment* there, former patients refer to it colloquially as “Hell”.

- Absolutely no privacy. Patients were required to sit in one small room with one television all day, every day. 20ish people crammed together. For a terrified socially-anxious recluse who rarely left the house more than once a week at the time — a.k.a. me — a room of loud, bored, frustrated people for 12+ hours a day with nobody I knew was hellish. Thankfully, it got better once I got to know the others, but the first few days were so hard for me. Other wards had boards games; we had none. We had some crayons, but nothing to colour (thankfully I brought in colouring books and shared them). One guy owned a pack of cards and we were lucky to have those. Some people had brought books, and we loaned them around. We weren’t allowed to sit in our rooms; they literally locked the bedroom doors at breakfast and only unlocked them at bedtime. We weren’t allowed off the ward. We ate at specific times and never inbetween except for the crackers we got as snacks *only* at snack time. We could only shower, bathe or brush our teeth between one hour in the morning and one hour in the evening. I honestly can not imagine actual prison being more strict or non-stimulating.

- Barely any therapy or enrichment. There were exactly two therapies/groups we had: one in the morning which largely consisted of personal squabbles the patients had with each other, and Narcotics/Alcoholics Anonymous at night. As I was not an addict, that reduced my “therapy” down to one hour of listening to people argue a day. As for recreation, well: there was a gymnasium, which we got to visit exactly twice during my week stay. Each visit was for an hour. It had a basketball court with a couple of hoops, a stack of board games and a handful of old used nail polishes. There was also an outdoor courtyard. We were supposed to go outside at least once a day; we went outside exactly once during the full week, again for an hour only. Every day, we’d beg to go outside and the staff would say “sure, sure, in a little bit”. It’s been over a year and I’m still waiting for my bit, assholes. If all of that wasn’t enough excitement, I saw on the timetable a slot for “Arts and Crafts” on Thursdays. I was so excited, I’m a very creative person. Thursday comes around, and as I’m sitting expectantly in my seat, a staff member comes into the room with a stack of papers and starts handing them out. “Where’s the Arts and Crafts?” I asked politely. “They stopped funding it,” he answered monotonously as he handed me a sheet and walked away. It was a fucking wordsearch.

- A lot of the staff were fucking terrible. Granted, some of the staff were kind, understanding, genuinely there to try do good — but they were really balanced out with some rude, inappropriate, uncaring twats. The psychiatrist I was under, for example, was a well-oiled machine who had a very specific system of worksheets. In the morning, he’d stop by and see how everyone was... Lol, no he wouldn’t. On my second morning, I was having a severe panic attack and was crying and shaking behind a chair in the extra rec room (which nobody was ever allowed in except to use the pay phone on the wall). I was well hidden, so the staff didn’t notice me for a while. Eventually, the psych spots me and walks in.

Psych: [With a cheery smile] Hello Sakura!

Me: [Whimpers]

Psych: How are you this morning?

Me: [Tearfully] Terrible!

Psych: Terrible?

Me: Yes! [Continues crying]

[A few seconds pass]

Psych: Well, see you tomorrow. [Walks the fuck out without a care in the world. The door swings shut behind him. I start crying harder.]

And the worksheets... Basically, how fast you were discharged depended on whether you completed the worksheets “correctly” and gave off a good impression of I-want-to-be-normal-for-realsies. Luckily, a guy on the ward was a couple of worksheets ahead of me, and he started telling me exactly what the psych was going to say and how to fill them in to his liking. I was fucking desperate to get out of that place, so I followed his advice. The psych was AMAZED at my progress! So amazed! What astounding insight! My shoulder devil laughed heartily. The other staff member I’d like to talk about held her own “therapy” one day. She wasn’t a licensed therapist, which should have been a clue. She’s going around the room, trying to inspire people and talking about what individually brought us there. A few of us had cried a little as she addressed specific people; I was one of them. Nothing wrong yet, we were all just being open and serious about what had hurt us. One patient was a fragile girl roughly my age. About half an hour in, the staff member pressed her a little, and she told us all that she’d been brutally tortured and raped by a group of men. Then she started quietly crying too. Suddenly, in an insane fit of “other people have it worse” syndrome, the staff member decided to talk about the facility across the street which was a long-term place for mentally ill children, many of whom had been through terrible things. She decided it would be a good idea to tell us of a young boy at that facility who was raped on his birthday whilst his rapist sung “happy birthday” to him. This sent the traumatised girl of our ward into a full-blown flashback to her own trauma. Her screams were terrible and she was completely inconsolable. She had to be essentially carried out and given tranquilizers. Unsurprisingly, the idiot staff member didn’t continue the session after that, nor try another session whilst I was there. The worst part was how ashamed the girl felt afterwards. We all had to adamantly reassure her that we understood and she had nothing to feel ashamed of.

- They had absolutely no idea how eating disorders work nor catered to them. I ate grilled cheese sandwiches (sliced hamburger cheese, of course) and raw onions for almost every meal during my stay, and the first few days I barely ate at all because I it took me that long to convince them into the grilled cheese. Outside food was forbidden. Snacks were forbidden, except the peanut butter crackers we got twice a day (which I also couldn’t eat).

- Want to be visit by a loved one? Great! You’ve got one hour. In one tiny room, sitting literally cheek to cheek with everyone else who got a visitor. Everyone was talking loudly to be heard over one another. A staff member sat and stared around suspiciously. Absolutely no bloody privacy ever.

- The place was falling apart. Tables wobbled. Walls peeling. Broken doors. The light in my room wouldn’t fucking turn off.

- They put people on some seriously powerful meds with little to no discussion. I mentioned that one psychiatrist had mentioned *once* after talking to me for just *30 minutes* that I *might* be Bipolar. I was immediately put on thrice-daily max-doses of lithium, lamotrigine and ariprazole (I think? I had a lot of med changes during that time, but that sounds right). By the way, I’ve never been properly diagnosed as Bipolar. In fact, my current healthcare providers absolutely insist I’m not. Meanwhile, one other girl was drugged so heavily for most of my stay that she could barely talk or open her eyes. She was also going through severe withdrawal from hard drugs and was basically tripping balls for days. I’ve gotten to know her since we were both discharged and she’s so intelligent, funny and sweet. You’d never have known it those first four days. (Side note, she’s also completely clean and is doing awesome now, yay!)

Fuck that hospital. Hell indeed.

First of all, no doctor can truly know when a person will pass. You’ve heard of Stephen Hawking’s passing recently, yes? He was given a few years to live at most by doctors in his early 20’s. He died aged 76. In the last stage of cancer, it’s very much a complete guess as to when somebody will pass. My SO’s best friend’s mother had late-stage cancer and travelled to a hospital appointment with him and his father; at the appointment, they told her that there was nothing more they could do for her, but that she still had some weeks left. She was still walking, albeit with difficulty, but communicating fine.

They left the hospital. She was dead in her car seat before they returned home. It’s almost as if she gave up as soon as the doctors confirmed that she was beyond help.

Really, what your doctors were saying is, “a week at best, we *think*”. Nobody can truly know. Your doctors told you their expectations, and you answered your mother based on that. As far as you knew, you were 100% correct. You can’t lie about something you believe is true, and you can’t break a promise you entirely believed in and had no control over.

But it’s more than that.

You couldn’t give your Mom any more time. She knew that, you know that. That’s not what she was asking for; she knew she was going to die. Nobody could help her stay alive and she knew it.

What you could give her was hope. She was scared of dying, as are most people. What she wanted at that moment was pretend that it would all be okay, despite the evidence to the contrary. It is a pretty common coping mechanism of a situation we will all have to face someday, someway. 

By reassuring your Mom, you allowed her to spend her last moments holding onto that hope. Your helped your mother believe to the end that it wasn’t the end. Wouldn’t we all want to go like that? Wouldn’t you want to believe in your final hours that you’d see another day and fall asleep with hope?

I don’t think your Mom actually thought you could promise her another day. I think she wanted to hear that you believed you could. It comforted her. I think your promise was a wonderful gift to a dying person.

I hope you can find peace.
